extracted.intended_audience: Authors of systematic reviews and meta-analysts (particularly Cochrane review authors)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for analysing data and undertaking meta-analyses in systematic reviews of interventions, covering choice of effect measures, statistical models, handling of special data types (rare events, skewed or missing data), heterogeneity, subgroup and sensitivity analyses, and reporting. Intended to inform decisions and best-practice implementation in review software (e.g. RevMan).

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not start here!
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not jump prematurely into a statistical analysis. Before undertaking meta-analysis, ensure that the review question is properly formulated; eligibility criteria are specified; studies have been identified and selected; appropriate data have been collected; risk of bias considered; intervention comparisons planned; and meaningful data to analyse have been decided.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Review authors should consult preceding chapters before a meta-analysis is undertaken; many judgements are needed prior to analysis and premature analysis can be misleading.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriateness of combining studies in a meta-analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: Thoughtfully consider whether it is appropriate to combine numerical results from all or some studies. A meta-analysis yields an overall statistic and confidence interval summarising intervention effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Advantages include improved precision, answering questions not posed by individual studies, and settling conflicting results; but statistical synthesis can be misused and does not guarantee validity. Consider study designs, within-study biases, variation across studies, and reporting biases before combining.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two-stage principle of meta-analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: Meta-analysis is typically a two-stage process: (1) calculate a summary statistic for each study to describe the observed intervention effect uniformly across studies; (2) calculate a combined intervention effect estimate as a weighted average of individual study effects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples of summary statistics: risk ratio for dichotomous data or difference between means for continuous. Weights determine contribution; use standard errors to derive confidence intervals and p-values; consider heterogeneity in whether studies estimate the same effect or a distribution of effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Generic inverse-variance approach
rubrics_metrics.description: Inverse-variance method gives each study a weight equal to the inverse of the variance (1/SE^2) of its effect estimate, so larger studies with smaller standard errors are given more weight.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This choice of weights minimizes the imprecision of the pooled estimate. RevMan implements inverse-variance and it is used for many data types; allows flexibility (enter estimates and SEs, e.g. log odds ratios) and analyses of cluster, crossover and non-randomized trials when appropriate adjustments are made.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fixed-effect meta-analysis (inverse-variance implementation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Fixed-effect (also called fixed/common/equal-effects) meta-analysis assumes all studies estimate the same underlying intervention effect; pooled estimate is a weighted average using inverse-variance weights.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Valid under the equal-effects assumption, though the pooled result can be interpreted without making that assumption. Required basic data: an estimate of the intervention effect and its standard error from each study.

rubrics_metrics.name: Random-effects meta-analysis (inverse-variance variations)
rubrics_metrics.description: Random-effects methods assume different studies estimate different, yet related, intervention effects drawn from a distribution (usually normal). Various inverse-variance based versions exist (e.g. DerSimonian and Laird and others with better properties).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Random-effects incorporate heterogeneity into pooling (see Section 10.10.4). Choice of estimator for between-study variance and methods to calculate uncertainty matter; interpret results carefully and consider prediction intervals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Performing inverse-variance meta-analyses in practice
rubrics_metrics.description: Most software performs inverse-variance meta-analyses; users typically supply summary data from each arm (e.g. 2×2 tables for dichotomous outcomes or means, SDs, Ns for continuous outcomes).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Using group summary data avoids manual calculation of effect estimates and enables methods targeted at different data types. RevMan's 'Generic inverse variance' allows entry of estimates and SEs, including log-scale data for ratio measures. Flexibility facilitates inclusion of properly analysed crossover, cluster-randomized and non-randomized trials, as well as ordinal, time-to-event or rate data.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choice of methods for dichotomous outcomes
rubrics_metrics.description: Four widely used methods: three fixed-effect methods (Mantel-Haenszel, Peto, inverse-variance) and one random-effects method (inverse-variance with variants). The Peto method only combines odds ratios; other methods can combine OR, RR or RD.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be aware of zero-cell problems for some methods (see rare events). Formulae and implementation differences influence bias and variance; selection depends on event sparsity, balance of group sizes, and expected effect sizes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mantel-Haenszel methods for dichotomous data
rubrics_metrics.description: Mantel-Haenszel are fixed-effect meta-analysis methods using a weighting scheme depending on chosen effect measure; they have better statistical properties when there are few events or small studies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because sparse data is common in Cochrane reviews, Mantel-Haenszel is generally preferable to inverse-variance in fixed-effect meta-analyses, though both give similar estimates in many situations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Peto odds ratio method: applicability and limits
rubrics_metrics.description: Peto’s method combines odds ratios using an inverse-variance approach with an approximate log-odds estimation and different weights; it can be viewed as a sum of O−E statistics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Works well when effects are small (OR close to 1), events uncommon, and treatment/comparator group sizes in studies are similar. Not recommended as the default because approximation can be biased when assumptions are violated. Peto needs no zero-cell corrections and performs well with very rare events and when log-rank based time-to-event and dichotomous data are combined. It underestimates very large effects but may still outperform alternatives for very rare events.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selecting effect measure for dichotomous outcomes (consistency, math properties, interpretability)
rubrics_metrics.description: Choice among risk ratio, odds ratio, risk difference, and number needed to treat depends on (1) consistency across studies/subgroups, (2) mathematical properties for valid meta-analysis (e.g. availability of variance estimators), and (3) ease of interpretation for users.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Empirical evidence: relative measures (RR, OR) are on average more consistent than absolute measures (RD). Avoid RD unless clear reason to expect consistency. Number needed to treat lacks a simple variance estimator and should not be used directly in meta-analysis. Recommend using RR (with careful event coding) or OR, and consider sensitivity analyses to assess effect of choice. Re-express relative effects as absolute measures (RD or NNT) using a baseline risk for interpretation and inclusion in 'Summary of findings' tables.

rubrics_metrics.name: Re-expressing relative effects to absolute effects
rubrics_metrics.description: It is often sensible to perform meta-analysis using a relative effect (RR or OR) and re-express results using an absolute statistic (risk difference or NNT) for interpretability; conversions require specification of baseline risk.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When baseline risk chosen is close to typical observed comparator risks, absolute estimates will be similar across summary statistics; otherwise predictions differ. Use these transformations (including converting OR to RR) for presentation in Summary of findings tables; convert confidence limits using same formulae.

rubrics_metrics.name: Meta-analysis of rare events: overall caution
rubrics_metrics.description: Rare event meta-analyses are challenging because many methods rely on large-sample approximations inappropriate when events are rare; a high proportion of studies may have zero events in one or both arms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: No single cutoff defines 'rare'. For very low event rates (e.g., <1%), performance of methods differs markedly. Carefully choose statistical methods; consider that detecting any signal may be priority over modelling heterogeneity. Avoid many inverse-variance and DerSimonian-Laird approaches for rare events.

rubrics_metrics.name: Handling studies with zero events in one arm
rubrics_metrics.description: Zero cells (no events in one group) cause computational problems when computing effect estimates and SEs (division by zero). Software often adds a fixed continuity correction (typically 0.5) to cells to avoid errors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fixed corrections bias estimates towards no difference and over-estimate variances (down-weighting studies), and can introduce directional bias when arm sizes are unequal. Alternatives include non-fixed corrections (e.g., Sweeting et al. proportional correction). Mantel-Haenszel requires corrections less often than inverse-variance; Peto method often avoids the need for corrections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Handling studies with zero events in both arms
rubrics_metrics.description: Standard practice is to exclude studies with no events in either arm from meta-analyses using odds ratios or risk ratios because they provide no information on direction or magnitude of relative effect; risk difference is defined as zero in this case but has drawbacks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Risk difference methods yield too-wide CIs and have poor power for rare events, making them unsuitable for many safety outcomes. Non-reporting of zero-event outcomes in trial reports complicates inclusion. Odds and RR methods naturally exclude such data, which may bias results if outcomes are omitted from publications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Validity of methods for rare events (simulation evidence and recommendations)
rubrics_metrics.description: Simulation studies show many commonly used methods are biased, have poor coverage, or low power when events are rare. Performance depends on comparator group risk, effect size, and balance of study arms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: At event rates below ~1% the Peto one-step OR method performed best under its assumptions (no substantial imbalance, small effects). For other situations, Mantel-Haenszel without zero-cell corrections, logistic regression, or exact methods may perform better (though not all available in RevMan). Methods to avoid with rare events include inverse-variance and DerSimonian-Laird random-effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Meta-analysis of continuous outcomes: normality and skewness considerations
rubrics_metrics.description: Standard methods assume approximately normal distribution of outcomes in each arm; this may be unimportant in very large trials but can matter in smaller studies or skewed outcomes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Review authors should consider possibility and implications of skewed data and use methods such as log-transformation or other approaches when appropriate (see Section 10.5.3 and related guidance).

rubrics_metrics.name: Choosing effect measure for continuous outcomes (MD vs SMD vs ratio of means)
rubrics_metrics.description: Mean difference (MD) is used when studies report outcomes on the same scale; standardized mean difference (SMD) when different scales measure the same construct; ratio of means is an alternative when measurements >0.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Understand different roles of SDs: in MD, SDs influence weights (studies with small SD get higher weight), appropriate if SD differences reflect measurement reliability; in SMD, SDs standardize differences and also influence weights — assumes between-study SD differences reflect scale differences, not real population variability. Consider interpretability (see Chapter 15).

rubrics_metrics.name: Meta-analysis of change scores vs post-intervention values
rubrics_metrics.description: Change-from-baseline analyses can be more efficient if they reduce between-person variability, but require baseline and follow-up measurements. ANCOVA (adjusted analyses including baseline as covariate) is preferred when available because it gives least biased and most precise estimates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Change scores and post-intervention values can legitimately be pooled on the MD scale (they estimate the same underlying effect on average in randomized trials), but combining them using SMD is problematic because SDs reflect different constructs. When mixing types, consider separate subgroups for clarity. Imputation of missing change SDs is sometimes necessary (see Chapter 6).

rubrics_metrics.name: Meta-analysis of skewed continuous data
rubrics_metrics.description: If outcome distributions are asymmetrical, analyses based on means may be inappropriate; skewness should be considered when analysing continuous outcomes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Options include transforming data (e.g., log transformation), combining results reported on transformed scales, or using non-parametric or alternative effect measures; detection of skewness can be aided by MECIR Box guidance and summary statistics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Combining dichotomous and continuous outcomes
rubrics_metrics.description: When evidence includes both dichotomous and continuous measures of the same construct, methods exist to combine them (e.g., convert effect measures), but require careful consideration and appropriate transformations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider whether a common metric is meaningful and how to convert scales (see Chapter 6 and Chapter 15 for methods and interpretability guidance).

rubrics_metrics.name: Meta-analysis of ordinal outcomes and measurement scales
rubrics_metrics.description: Ordinal outcomes and measurement scales may be dichotomized or analysed using ordinal methods; choice of cut-point for dichotomizing short ordinal scales affects results.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors should justify cut-points and consider loss of information; alternatives include ordinal meta-analytic methods or presenting results across scale categories. Consider whether SMD is appropriate when scales measure the same construct.

rubrics_metrics.name: Meta-analysis of counts and rates
rubrics_metrics.description: Pooling incidence rates when follow-up durations vary requires methods for rates; explicit methods exist for combining rates and account for varying follow-up.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose appropriate model (e.g., Poisson-based approaches) and account for person-time denominators; consult methods literature and examples (e.g., Guevara et al.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Meta-analysis of time-to-event outcomes
rubrics_metrics.description: Time-to-event outcomes are commonly combined using log hazard ratios (or approximations from survival curves/log-rank tests).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where necessary, extract log hazard ratios and SEs from published data or use approximations; Peto method can combine dichotomous studies with time-to-event analyses when log-rank tests have been used.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition, identification and measurement of heterogeneity
rubrics_metrics.description: Heterogeneity refers to variation in results across studies that may be more than expected by chance. Identify and quantify heterogeneity using statistics (e.g., I^2, tau^2) and visual inspection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider clinical, methodological and statistical sources. Use measures like I^2 to quantify inconsistency; remember many Cochrane reviews lack enough studies to reliably investigate causes. Consider impact on choice between fixed-effect and random-effects models.

rubrics_metrics.name: Strategies for addressing heterogeneity
rubrics_metrics.description: Options include subgroup analyses, meta-regression, using random-effects models to allow for between-study variation, exploring causes through study-level characteristics, and conducting sensitivity analyses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Random-effects assume effects follow a distribution; interpret with care. Use prediction intervals to present between-study variation. Selection of heterogeneity variance estimators and method for uncertainty estimation matters (see Veroniki et al., Hartung-Knapp, REML alternatives).

rubrics_metrics.name: Investigating heterogeneity: subgroup analyses and effect modification
rubrics_metrics.description: Subgroup analyses estimate effects within subsets; meta-regression explores effect modification across study-level covariates. Interaction tests assess differences between subgroups.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clearly define subgroup hypotheses (preferably a priori), limit number of comparisons, be cautious about ecological bias in meta-regression, and use instruments/criteria (e.g., ICEMAN) to assess credibility of effect modification analyses. Interpret subgroup/meta-regression findings cautiously and avoid over-interpretation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selection of study characteristics for subgroup analyses and meta-regression
rubrics_metrics.description: Choose study-level characteristics that are plausible effect modifiers, relevant to clinical questions, and justifiable based on prior knowledge or theory.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid data-driven fishing; pre-specify where possible; consider power and the risk of spurious findings; when characteristics are continuous consider appropriate modelling (e.g., meta-regression, dose-response methods).

rubrics_metrics.name: Investigating effect of underlying risk and dose-response analyses
rubrics_metrics.description: Explore whether baseline or underlying risk explains heterogeneity and examine dose-response relationships where applicable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use appropriate methods (e.g., trend estimation, meta-regression). Be cautious of confounding and ecological bias; interpret relationships as hypothesis-generating unless robustly supported.

rubrics_metrics.name: Handling missing data in meta-analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider types of missing data (participant-level lost to follow-up, unreported outcomes, missing SDs, etc.) and their implications. Decide assumptions about missing outcome data and whether to use adjusted or unadjusted estimates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply general principles for dealing with missing data (imputation methods, sensitivity analyses). For continuous outcomes impute missing SDs when necessary (see Chapter 6). For participant missingness consider impact on estimates and incorporate sensitivity analyses to examine robustness (see MECIR Box and referenced guidance).

rubrics_metrics.name: Bayesian approaches to meta-analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: Bayesian random-effects and other Bayesian methods provide alternative frameworks for meta-analysis, including incorporation of informative priors for heterogeneity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bayesian methods can be useful for small numbers of studies or to incorporate external information; tools and packages (e.g., bayesmeta) and comparative studies exist. Carefully consider choice of priors and sensitivity to them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sensitivity analyses to assess robustness
rubrics_metrics.description: Use sensitivity analyses to examine whether overall findings are robust to potentially influential decisions (choice of methods, assumptions about missing data, effect measures, corrections for zero cells, inclusion/exclusion decisions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pre-specify where possible, but many sensitivity analyses arise during the review. Report sensitivity analyses succinctly (summary table recommended); rarely necessary to produce individual forest plots for each sensitivity analysis. Distinguish sensitivity analyses from subgroup analyses (sensitivity analyses do not estimate effects for removed studies; subgroup analyses provide subgroup estimates and formal comparisons).

rubrics_metrics.name: Key analysis decisions and checklist of assumptions to make explicit
rubrics_metrics.description: Explicitly decide and document key analysis choices: fixed-effect vs random-effects; effect measures for dichotomous (OR/RR/RD) and continuous (MD/SMD); handling of change vs post-intervention data; approaches for rare events; imputation choices for missing SDs; assumptions for clustered/crossover trials; baseline risk assumptions for absolute effect re-expression; whether adjusted or unadjusted estimates are used.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These decisions can be pre-specified in the protocol where possible. Many are suitable for sensitivity analysis. When decisions materially affect conclusions, consider follow-up actions (obtain extra information, contact authors, consider IPD) and interpret results with caution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reporting and graphical presentation recommendations
rubrics_metrics.description: Meta-analyses are usually illustrated with forest plots showing study effect estimates, CIs, weights (block sizes) and the pooled diamond; present prediction intervals for random-effects to show between-study variation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Forest plots help visual interpretation; block area and CIs convey weight and precision. Use Summary of findings tables to present re-expressed absolute effects and certainty of evidence. Report sensitivity analyses concisely (summary table) and justify choices of methods and effect measures in text.
